/-!
# Erdős Problem 189

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/189](https://www.erdosproblems.com/189)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Affine EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos189

/-- Erdős problem 189 asked whether the below holds for all rectangles. -/
def Erdos189For (P : ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → Prop) (A : ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ) :=
    ∀ᵉ (n > 0) (colouring : ℝ² → Fin n), ∃ colour, ∀ area > (0 : ℝ), ∃ a b c d,
      {a, b, c, d} ⊆ colouring⁻¹' {colour} ∧
      IsCcwConvexPolygon ![a, b, c, d] ∧
      A a b c d = area ∧
      P a b c d

/--
If $\mathbb{R}^2$ is finitely coloured then must there exist some colour class which contains the
vertices of a rectangle of every area?

Graham, "On Partitions of 𝔼ⁿ", Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 28, 89-91 (1980).
(See "Concluding Remarks" on page 96.)

Solved (with answer `False`, as formalised below) in:
Vjekoslav Kovač, "Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume", 2023
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.09973
In fact, Kovač's colouring is even Jordan measurable (the topological boundary of each
monochromatic region is Lebesgue measurable and has measure zero).

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev and Kovac using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos189.lean"]
theorem erdos_189 :
    answer(False) ↔ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, b, c].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, b, c].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, c, d].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, c, d].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, d, a].direction)
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c) := by
  sorry

/-- Graham claims this is "easy to see". -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 51]
theorem erdos_189.variants.square :
    ¬ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, b, c].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, b, c].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, c, d].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, c, d].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, d, a].direction ∧
        dist a b = dist b c)
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c) := by
  sorry

/--
Seems to be open, as of January 2025.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 51]
theorem erdos_189.variants.parallelogram :
    ¬ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b] ∥ line[ℝ, c, d] ∧
        line[ℝ, a, d] ∥ line[ℝ, b, c])
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c * (∡ a b c).sin) := by
  sorry

end Erdos189

findings.description: The source leaves the parallelogram version as an open yes/no question and does not conjecture an answer. The Lean instead states `¬ Erdos189For (fun a b c d ↦ line[ℝ, a, b] ∥ line[ℝ, c, d] ∧ line[ℝ, a, d] ∥ line[ℝ, b, c]) (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c * (∡ a b c).sin)` with tag `research open`. That commits to the NEGATIVE answer: some finite colouring has no colour class containing parallelograms of every area. If the answer turns out positive, the source's question is simply answered 'yes', but this Lean theorem is false. So the declaration asserts a resolution the source does not pose, rather than stating the question. The docstring ("Seems to be open, as of January 2025.") neither states the question nor gives a conjectured direction. The rest of the statement is sound. The predicate is convex position plus both pairs of opposite sides parallel, which forces a parallelogram. The area term `dist a b * dist b c * (∡ a b c).sin` equals the cross product (a−b)×(c−b); I proved this in Lean, and it is positive under `IsCcwConvexPolygon`. Parallelograms of every area satisfy the predicate (checked in Lean). The only defect is the fixed polarity. This differs from a negated conjecture: there is no `answer(sorry)` slot to absorb the unknown answer.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/189 (Wayback snapshot 2026-07-14, and its LaTeX source): "The same question can be asked for parallelograms." ... "The question for parallelograms remains open." Kovač, arXiv:2309.09973, §1.3 'Parallelograms and parallelotopes', states it as a question: "If R^2 is finitely colored then must there exist some color-class which contains the vertices of a parallelogram of every given area?". He adds: "Unable to answer the question in Problem ... Problem could be difficult, especially if it turns out that the claim has a positive answer." He quotes Erdős–Graham [EG80, p. 15]: "Is this also true for rectangles? Or perhaps parallelograms?". Graham, JCTA 28 (1980), Concluding Remarks p. 96: "does Theorem 1 apply to parallelograms ...? Rhombuses? Rectangles?". Kovač, erdosproblems forum thread 189 (10 Aug 2025), gives only partial results (thin parallelograms, infinitely many directions); the question is still open.
findings.suggested_fix:
State the question with an answer slot, and have the docstring state it:
/-- The same question for parallelograms: if $\mathbb{R}^2$ is finitely coloured, must some colour class contain the vertices of a parallelogram of every area? This is open. -/
@[category research open, AMS 5 51]
theorem erdos_189.variants.parallelogram :

      (fun a b c d ↦ line[ℝ, a, b] ∥ line[ℝ, c, d] ∧ line[ℝ, a, d] ∥ line[ℝ, b, c])
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c * (∡ a b c).sin) := by
  sorry

findings.description: Reference slip in the docstring. It cites Graham, 'On Partitions of 𝔼ⁿ', J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 28, "89-91" (1980), then sends the reader to the Concluding Remarks "on page 96", which lies outside that range. The paper occupies pages 89–97. The mathematics is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/189 reference list: "[Gr80] Graham, R. L., On partitions of E^n. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1980), 89-97." The bibliography of Kovač arXiv:2309.09973 gives PAGES = {89--97}, MR0558877. The scanned paper (mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_03_partitions.pdf) has page numbers up to 97: Concluding Remarks on p. 96, continuing on p. 97.

reformulations.difference: The source says 'the vertices of a rectangle of every area'. The Lean encodes 'a rectangle of area A' as: `IsCcwConvexPolygon ![a,b,c,d]` (strictly convex position with one fixed orientation sign), orthogonal directions for the line pairs ab/bc, bc/cd and cd/da (only three right angles), and `dist a b * dist b c = A`. `answer(False) ↔ Erdos189For …` stands for the negative answer. A reader might worry about the single allowed orientation, the missing fourth right angle, or the area formula.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (⇐) Label any non-degenerate (possibly rotated) rectangle cyclically. All oriented angles ∡ p_i p_j p_k with i<j<k then have the same sign, and reversing the labelling flips that sign. So one cyclic labelling satisfies `IsCcwConvexPolygon`. Every cyclic labelling satisfies the three perpendicularity conditions and has dist a b · dist b c = area. (⇒) `IsCcwConvexPolygon` forces distinct, non-collinear vertices. Write u=b−a, v=c−b, w=d−c. From u·v=0 and v·w=0 with v≠0 in 2D, u∥w. Then w·(d−a)=0 with w≠0 forces w=−u, so d=a+c−b: a parallelogram with a right angle at b, i.e. a rectangle, and |ab|·|bc| is its area. The name 'Ccw' is actually clockwise in the standard orientation of ℝ² (checked in Lean), which does not matter by the same relabelling argument. The quantifier order ∃ colour ∀ area matches 'some colour class which contains … of every area'. Kovač's 25-colouring with no monochromatic area-1 rectangle gives ¬Erdos189For. The linked external Lean proof proves exactly `Erdos189For … ↔ False`. Lean checks in /workspace/review: rectangles of every positive area satisfy the predicate (axis-parallel witness). From the predicate I proved d = a + c − b. A right trapezoid (the leak Alexeev reported in an earlier version) is excluded by the current third condition. The general '(⇐) for every rotated rectangle' direction is argued, not machine-checked.

review.notes:
No problems were found in the main statement. With all three perpendicularity conditions, the predicate is exactly 'a rectangle, arbitrarily rotated'. This version already fixes the misformalization Boris Alexeev reported on the erdosproblems forum (19 Dec 2025): with only AB⊥BC and BC⊥CD, right trapezoids got through. I confirmed in Lean that such a trapezoid is now excluded, and that the predicate forces d = a + c − b.

Square variant: Graham 1980, p. 96 says \"Of course, it is easy to see that it cannot hold for squares.\" Here 'it' is his lattice Theorem 1. The Lean states the continuous-plane analogue (¬ Erdos189For for squares), which fits the framing of Erdős #189. It is true: take a 7-colouring of the plane with no monochromatic unit distance; then no colour class contains a square of area 1. Squares of every area satisfy the predicate (checked in Lean).

The website's remark \"It is not true for rhombuses\" is not formalized. That omission is fine: Kovač says on the forum that he knows no counterexample for rhombuses, and Graham listed rhombuses as open in 1980 and again in 2015.

Parallelogram variant: the only issue is the fixed polarity. The area term reduces to the cross product (a−b)×(c−b), proved in Lean, and slanted parallelograms of every area satisfy the predicate.

Library naming: `IsCcwConvexPolygon` (FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Geometry/2d.lean) actually describes clockwise polygons in the standard orientation of ℝ². In Lean, the standard counter-clockwise unit square fails it and its reversal satisfies it. This does not affect this file, because every predicate used is invariant under the relabelling.

Status: the categories match the source. The main problem is disproved and verified in Lean (erdosproblems: DISPROVED (LEAN); the formal_proof link proves the statement). The square variant is solved/easy. The parallelogram question is still open per the 2026 erdosproblems snapshot and Kovač's 2025 comments; I found no later resolution. No status issues.

not_demonstrated.reason: It fixes the negative answer to a problem that is still open, so neither the statement nor its negation has a short proof. The predicate is satisfiable for every area (non-vacuous) and the area formula is correct, so there is no vacuity or bad definition to exhibit. The defect is only the fixed polarity where `answer(sorry)` belongs.

submission.summary: No trivial proof or disproof is possible, and I did not create a trivial-proof file. The one misformalization I reported (erdos_189.variants.parallelogram) asserts a definite negative answer to the open question of whether every finite colouring of ℝ² has a colour class containing parallelograms of every area. Settling it either way is research-level. In my scratch experiments the statement is non-vacuous and its predicate and area term are correct. So the defect is one of stating the problem, not something a few Lean lines can prove or refute.
submission.gave_up_reason: The only misformalization I reported is Erdos189.erdos_189.variants.parallelogram. It is a fixed-polarity statement (`¬ Erdos189For …`, i.e. the answer 'no') of a question the source leaves open. The defect is that it commits to an unknown answer, not that it is trivially true or false. Proving it would settle the open Erdős–Graham parallelogram question negatively, and refuting it would settle it positively; either needs real mathematics. Nothing degenerate can be exploited. In scratch experiments, parallelograms of every positive area satisfy the predicate, so `Erdos189For` is not vacuous. The area term reduces to the true parallelogram area, (a−b)×(c−b). No definition misbehaves on a concrete input. The minor finding (page range '89-91' instead of '89–97' in a docstring) is not something Lean can show. I never created /workspace/review/trivial_proof.lean, so there is nothing to delete, and nothing under /opt/formal-conjectures was modified.

submission.summary: Changed `erdos_189.variants.parallelogram` from `¬ Erdos189For …`, which asserted a negative answer to an open question, to `answer(sorry) ↔ Erdos189For …`. The parallelogram predicate and area term are unchanged. Its docstring now states the question as posed ("if ℝ² is finitely coloured, must there exist some colour class which contains the vertices of a parallelogram of every area?"). It keeps "Seems to be open, as of January 2025." and the `research open, AMS 5 51` attributes, since the parallelogram case is still open per erdosproblems.com (2026 snapshot) and Kovač. Also fixed the trivial, safe docstring slip in `erdos_189`: Graham's page range "89-91" is now "89-97". No statement other than the parallelogram variant changed. Compile check: `lake env lean --json` on the file reports only three `declaration uses 'sorry'` warnings. With the lakefile's FormalConjectures lint options passed as flags, it reports nothing, in both the default and `google.answer=postpone` modes. `answer(sorry)` elaborates to `True ↔ …` in the default mode, as for every other `answer(sorry)` problem (e.g. Erdős 488). Nothing else under /opt/formal-conjectures was modified; `lakefile.toml` and `run/` were already modified before the session. The original file is backed up at /workspace/review/189.lean.orig.
